name: Nottingham

licensing.selective: Selective licensing covers most of the city (about 30,000 privately rented homes in wards including Aspley, Basford, Castle, Meadows, Radford, Sherwood and St Ann's) from 1 December 2023 to 30 November 2028; the council's postcode checker shows whether a home is inside it. It follows a first scheme that ran from 2018 to 2023.
licensing.additional: Citywide additional HMO licensing since January 2024: HMOs of three or more unrelated people forming two or more households need a licence, as well as the larger HMOs under mandatory licensing.
licensing.fee: £1,607 for a standard additional HMO licence (up to 9 bedrooms, from April 2026), £1,210 for landlords accredited under the Nottingham Rental Standard, paid in two parts

rent.text: £1,015 a month (ONS, September 2026), up 1.7% on a year earlier

price.text: £190,000 (UK HPI, August 2026, provisional), down 1.8% on a year earlier

privateRentedShare.text: 28.6% of households rent privately (Census 2021), up from 23.1% in 2011

councilTax.text: £2,342.08 Band D for the City Council's own share (2026/27, up 3.5%); about £2,755 in total with the police and fire precepts

housing: Nottingham has a large private rented sector, with more than a quarter of households renting privately in 2021. Two universities mean many student HMOs, especially in the Victorian terraces of Lenton, Radford and Dunkirk, alongside purpose-built student blocks in the city centre. The Arboretum and Forest Fields have large Victorian houses split into flats and bedsits, while the outer estates such as Aspley, Bilborough and Clifton are mostly inter-war and post-war council-built homes. Most privately rented homes in the city need a selective or HMO licence.
checkinTips: Student HMOs in Lenton and Radford: photograph each bedroom lock, fire doors and closers, alarms and the shared kitchen and bathroom separately, and note the HMO licence number.
Selective licensing: check the property's licence and photograph smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, as these are licence conditions.
Victorian houses split into flats in the Arboretum and Forest Fields: record communal hallways, meter cupboards and the key count for each door.
Lace Market warehouse conversions and city-centre blocks: note fob counts, intercom, parking and bike stores, and any exposed brick or timber.
Terraces with small back yards: photograph damp at the base of walls, yard gates and where the bins are kept.
Inter-war homes in Aspley and Bilborough: photograph gardens, fences, sheds and older boilers.
tenantHelp: Tenants can report disrepair, damp or unsafe conditions in privately rented homes, or a home that should be licensed and isn't, to Nottingham City Council's private sector housing team.
